writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Frequency-Balanced Window when it asks for character replacement and bounded edits. Here the concrete task is: With at most one replacement, return the longest equal-character substring length. The visible input `AABABBA` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Choose this family when a valid window can be repaired by moving one boundary; non-monotone constraints may need a different method. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Track the dominant count so replacements needed equal window length minus that count. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A window is a contiguous interval with a maintained summary. Describe what entering the right edge adds and what leaving the left edge removes. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) time · O(alphabet) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `4` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test an empty window, a window spanning the whole input, and a case where the left edge must advance several times. Represent bounds as a half-open range when possible. Keep counts and the window length in sync when shrinking it. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
